name: Priya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does your ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I usually arrive to three client messages about wages that do not match the payroll sheet. I prepare accounts and tax returns at the firm, check the figures with the client, and send the file to the partner for sign-off. I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and after years in this work I still prefer a paper trail to a quick guess; the late corrections wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and what tools do you use now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Daniel runs the grocery shelves, and our school-age children Ruthie and Ben both need us at pickup. We have a mortgage, but my experienced accountant pay is below the usual rate, there is less than a month of expenses saved, and few firms nearby offer similar work. I have never used AI tools; I rely on client records, colleagues, and the staff association when hours get unfair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small sorter would leave the payroll deadlines and client calls where they are. My worry would still be the mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my colleagues that a receipt tool is fine only if we can trace every number and keep a person responsible. I would also say the firm should count the extra checking time, not just the typing it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is no easy year for me even with little AI change. I earn below the usual rate for an experienced accountant, we have less than a month saved, and only a few firms nearby hire people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing the payroll accounts and returns under our current review process. I would cancel the paid television package this month and transfer the freed fifteen from each monthly wage into a mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary bills, not about a little receipt software. One sick week could leave our loan payment short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What else makes the budget tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Daniel supervises the grocery shelves and our two children need school supplies every term. His pay covers part of the mortgage, but we need both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise the pay issue at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the actual unpaid review hours to the staff association with a colleague. I want a wage discussion grounded in what the firm has asked us to do, not a vague complaint.

I would ask the firm to count **extra checking time** alongside saved typing.
think: My **below-standard pay** and under-one-month reserve already threaten the mortgage.
Few nearby firms make a quick **job move** unlikely.
do: Keep the current **payroll review** process for client accounts.
Cancel **paid television** and transfer fifteen monthly to the mortgage buffer.
Bring logged **review hours** to the staff association with a colleague.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills even without radical AI.
S0.quote: One sick week could leave our loan payment short.
fieldNote: Her anxiety precedes AI: **low pay** and tiny reserves make a missed week material.
She seeks a **documented wage discussion** through colleagues rather than treating a receipt tool as the central issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and customer answers are most of our office. I would expect the firm to ask the same people to cover more files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell staff that the firm should show which returns the software writes and who is accountable for mistakes. The staff association should ask for paid training and notice before anyone loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours could be cut as the firm moves payroll checks to a system, and Daniel’s grocery wage cannot carry the mortgage alone. With less than a month saved, I cannot wait through a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would join two colleagues at the staff association meeting to ask for written notice and paid training. If the firm offers a supervised class on its approved tool during paid hours, I would attend; if my hours fall in the first year, I would apply only to posted payroll jobs with written wages, hours, and a start date that cover our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my pay could shrink before I have another offer. I know the payroll rules, but I have never used AI and need a person beside me for the first live case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current files and use the professional body’s free written examples to learn the checks, without putting a client return through AI myself. I would not pay for a course while the mortgage buffer is so small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any posted payroll job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, an advertisement is only a lead. I would wait for a written offer that names the wage, shift hours, and start date before handing in notice.

say: I would ask for **written notice** before paid hours are cut.
I would seek **paid supervised training** with a named person checking live work.
think: My own **payroll hours** could fall when the firm automates first checks.
Daniel’s grocery wage cannot carry the **mortgage** without mine for long.
do: Join colleagues at a **staff association meeting** this month.
Take **paid supervised AI training** if offered; use free written examples while employed otherwise.
Apply for **posted payroll work** after hours fall only with written bill-covering terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own wage.
S1.quote: I would wait for a written offer that names the wage, shift hours, and start date before handing in notice.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI**, so her training requires an approved tool and paid supervision.
Her search starts only after **lost hours** and cannot end in resignation before written wage, shift, and date terms.

steps.text: Join staff association meeting with two colleagues for notice and paid training
Take paid supervised AI class if offered; otherwise study free examples while employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would barely cover two tax seasons. Robots later do not keep an accounting desk alive in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm owes clients a named signer and staff a notice period when AGI handles accounts and payroll in 2028. I would also tell my neighbours that robots around 2031 are later, so my screen work faces the first shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my accounting role or most of my pay to go, and Daniel’s grocery work may feel robot pressure three years later. Less than a month in savings would not carry our mortgage through even a short search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would cancel the planned summer trip and use its monthly savings to build a cash buffer, while joining the staff association’s severance meeting. If I lose my accounting pay in the first year after 2028, I would ask my mother Ruth to cover school pickup temporarily and apply for an advertised school payroll post only if a written wage, hours, and start date cover our mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and keep waking at night to count our bills. I can ask for terms and keep working now, but I cannot invent a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ruth be able to do pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother Ruth lives nearby and has offered one term of help, not an open-ended arrangement. I would take her help only if a real job offer needs that pickup time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school post is also automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would treat it as a paid bridge, not a safe career. I would keep my current salary while it exists and apply only when a real opening and wage are posted.

say: I would demand a **named signer** and notice before the 2028 change.
I would separate **2028 desk work** from robots arriving around 2031.
think: I expect my **accounting wage** to disappear or shrink sharply.
Our under-one-month **reserve** cannot carry the mortgage through a search.
do: Cancel the **summer trip** and deposit its monthly cost into cash.

Seek **posted school payroll** after layoff only with written shifts/start date and wages covering mortgage and childcare.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about immediate household income.
S2.quote: I can ask for terms and keep working now, but I cannot invent a vacancy.
fieldNote: Her expected **2028 screen-work loss** precedes later robot pressure on Daniel’s grocery job.
Ruth’s pickup offer is **one term only** and depends on a real job with written wage and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let us argue for rules before a cut and try another kind of client work. The mortgage still comes due each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the staff association to seek a funded route into payroll compliance checks and clear notice before posts disappear. Our accounts screens face AGI in 2031, while robots reach hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think some of my review hours may vanish, but five years could let me build a different record if the firm pays for practice. I would not spend our tiny buffer on a qualification that has no paid job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in the professional body’s payroll compliance module only if the firm pays its fee and gives paid study hours, then handle one supervised client query quarterly if my manager Nessa assigns paid time. I would transfer fifteen from each monthly wage into the mortgage buffer; in the first year after 2031 I would take a posted compliance role only if written pay, hours, and a start date cover our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the work could shrink before the module leads to anything. I would keep my present pay if no funded class or real vacancy appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm refuses the fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would study the professional body’s free case notes after dinner and keep preparing returns while the current salary lasts. I would not take a loan for a payroll compliance module.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would watch the children for evening study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel could cover the older child’s pickup, but we would need a class after his grocery shift for the younger one. If the timetable conflicts, I would wait for the next free notes session rather than pay for care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years takes our children through school. I could build a record without leaving a wage behind on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm has time to fund real staff learning before AGI reaches accounting desks in 2036. Robots around 2039 are later for hands-on work, and clients still deserve a named answer to a wrong tax bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect routine payroll checks to pay less by 2036, but I could have experience explaining compliance cases to clients. With less than a month saved now, I cannot feel relaxed just because the date is far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing payroll returns now and transfer fifteen from each monthly wage into cash until we have three months of expenses. I would work through paid compliance queries only if Nessa assigns them; if my accounting post contracts in the first year after 2036, I would take a posted compliance job only with a written wage, hours, and start date covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our thin buffer today, although the desk change gives me more warning. The mortgage does not wait ten years for us to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait for the firm to offer training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff association to negotiate paid time for client queries and a notice period before any cut. If Nessa never assigns cases, I would keep my current files and use the free case notes while still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Ruthie and Ben that I am building a buffer before changing any job. They should not have to carry our worry about the loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my accounting pay could end before we have even a month of bills saved. A written notice period, paid compliance training, and a real job with mortgage-covering wages would help. We might need short-term mortgage support if the post ends before another starts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays for the extra checking when a quick system makes a wrong tax bill. I would bring that question to the staff association before the firm changes the rota. A saving on a spreadsheet can become a bill at someone’s kitchen table.

headlineQuote: A saving on a spreadsheet can become a bill at someone’s kitchen table.
portrait: Priya is a **43-year-old** experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who checks payroll accounts.
She has **low pay**, under one month saved, a grocery-supervisor partner, two school-age children, and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI** and lives near few other firms offering similar accounting work.
She uses **staff association** action to seek notice, paid learning, and fair review workloads.
The **2028** shock alarms her; even the slow picture leaves the present mortgage and thin cushion worrying.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her accounting wage before she has a month of bills saved.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, paid compliance training, a mortgage-covering vacancy, and short-term support if needed.
